lede: The 7-year auction stopped at 5.085% with the thinnest demand of 2026 but no real tail; long yields set another 2026 high, stocks were flat, and yields and oil are easing this morning.
geo_headlines: THE SEVEN-YEAR AUCTION DREW THE THINNEST DEMAND OF 2026 BUT DID NOT TAIL. Treasury's auction record shows a 5.085% stop, bid-to-cover 2.42 and indirect bidders at 57.20% of accepted competitive bids. Against the eight regular seven-year auctions earlier this year, that is the lowest bid-to-cover and the lowest indirect share. Dow Jones calls it the highest seven-year auction yield since April 1993, but the when-issued was 5.078%, so the tail was only about 0.7 basis points.

LONG YIELDS MADE ANOTHER 2026 HIGH AND THE CURVE STEEPENED. Treasury's curve file for Thursday has the ten-year at 5.18% (up 7 basis points), the thirty-year at 5.47% (up 7) and the two-year at 4.87% (up 2), all sole highs for the year. The gap between the two- and ten-year widened to 31 basis points from 26. CNBC puts the late ten-year near 5.225%, the highest since June 2007. This morning it is back near 5.17%.

STOCKS FINISHED FLAT AND THE AI TRADE SPLIT IN TWO. The S&P 500 slipped 0.02% to 7,704.13 and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.03% to 30,478.86. Meta rose 4.50% while Oracle fell 3.48% after sending a force majeure notice on a Blue Owl-developed New Mexico data center; Oracle says the project remains on track. After the bell Akamai jumped about 19% on an 11.6 billion dollar, seven-year cloud deal with Anthropic, having closed down 6.78%.

OCTOBER HIKE ODDS EDGED UP AGAIN AFTER WILLIAMS. CME FedWatch now prices a 70.9% chance of a quarter-point hike on October 28, up from 68.6% a day earlier. New York Fed President Williams said in London that another hike this year is a reasonable expectation. Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate moved above 7% for the first time since January 2025.

OIL GAVE BACK PART OF THURSDAY'S JUMP ON US-IRAN TALKS. Brent settled up 3.4% on Thursday and is about 1% lower this morning after Reuters reported negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path in which Hormuz reopens and the blockade is lifted. The risk has not gone away: Saudi Arabia intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu.

TOKYO ROSE FOR A FIFTH DAY WHILE HONG KONG FELL. The Nikkei gained 1.30% to 66,364.20 and the Topix 1.31%. The Hang Seng fell 1.01% to 24,510.09. Mainland China, Taiwan and Korea were closed for holidays. Europe opened higher, with the CAC 40 up 0.45%, and German consumer confidence from GfK suffered what the survey called a significant setback.

COSTCO BEAT AND THE STOCK BARELY MOVED. Costco reported fiscal fourth-quarter earnings of 6.75 dollars a share on revenue of 95.7 billion dollars, ahead of the roughly 6.55 dollars analysts expected. The shares closed down 0.91% before the report and were down 0.23% after hours.
client_frame_short: The auction the bond market was bracing for came and went without breaking anything. The 7-year sold at 5.085%, the highest since 1993 per Dow Jones, with the thinnest demand of the year, but it tailed by less than a basis point. Stocks finished flat, and this morning yields are a touch lower and futures a touch higher. **For clients, the point is that the market is absorbing supply at a higher price, not refusing it.** Today's reads are durable goods at 8:30 and final Michigan sentiment at 10:00; the bigger test is August PCE on Wednesday, Sept 30.
client_frame:
The one-line version for clients this morning is that Thursday was the stress test for the bond market and it passed, at a price. The $44 billion seven-year auction stopped at 5.085%, which Dow Jones calls the highest seven-year auction yield since April 1993. Treasury's own record shows a bid-to-cover of 2.42 and indirect bidders at 57.20%, the lowest of the nine regular seven-year auctions this year on both counts. But the when-issued yield was 5.078%, so the tail was about 0.7 basis points. Yesterday I said a tail above two basis points would turn this into something disorderly. It did not happen.

The curve still moved higher. Treasury's curve file has the ten-year at 5.18%, up 7 basis points, and the thirty-year at 5.47%, each a new high for 2026, while the two-year rose only 2 basis points to 4.87%. That is a steepener: the long end is demanding more compensation, which is a term-premium story rather than a Fed story. CNBC puts the ten-year's late high near 5.225%, the highest since June 2007, which is within a few basis points of the 5.25% level I flagged. This morning it has eased back to about 5.17% and, per Bloomberg, global yields are cooling with it.

Stocks shrugged. The S&P 500 slipped 0.02% and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.03%, so the S&P is 1.22% below its August 13 record and the Nasdaq 100 is 0.82% below its September 22 record. Underneath, the AI trade split. Meta rose 4.50%, Oracle fell 3.48% after a force majeure notice on a New Mexico data center that it says remains on track, and Akamai rose about 19% after hours on an $11.6 billion, seven-year cloud deal with Anthropic. The lesson for clients is dispersion: the same theme is producing winners and losers on the same day, which argues for breadth rather than a single bet.

The Fed piece keeps drifting hawkish. CME FedWatch has a 70.9% chance of an October hike, up from 68.6%, and New York Fed President Williams called another hike this year a reasonable expectation. The household version of this story is mortgages: Freddie Mac's 30-year rate is above 7% for the first time since January 2025. For clients with cash to put to work, high-quality bonds now pay real income. For clients carrying variable-rate debt, it is a reason to look at terms.

Oil is the swing factor. Brent settled up 3.4% Thursday and is about 1% lower this morning after Reuters reported US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path to reopening Hormuz. The Houthi missiles Saudi Arabia intercepted overnight are a reminder that a headline can reverse that. Gold is up about 1.1% as yields ease.

So the client framing is this. The bond market is repricing, but it is clearing: auctions are selling, stocks are flat, and volatility is low, with the VIX at 15.67. That is an orderly adjustment to higher rates, and it is an opportunity to lock in yield. What would change my view is a ten-year close above 5.25%, or a hot August PCE report on Wednesday, Sept 30, that lifts the roughly 30% odds FedWatch now gives a third hike by January. Either would turn a repricing into a problem for equity valuations.
